analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using shared pricing algorithms to inflate rents.
analysis.headline: S. 3692 was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 30, 2024, never received a hearing, vote, or floor action, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for rental property owners to use software services that collect prices and lease data from many landlords and recommend rents back to them, treating such shared pricing algorithms as a per se violation of the Sherman Act, the nation's strongest antitrust law. It would let the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private tenants sue, and it would let tenants recover triple their damages and escape forced-arbitration clauses that block class actions. The bill defines a covered rental property owner as anyone leasing four or more residential units.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters. The bill targets rent-setting software that pools pricing data from competing landlords and recommends rents, a practice regulators say can push apartment rents above what competition would produce. Tenants would gain new tools to sue, with triple damages, attorney fees, and the ability to bypass pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a per se Sherman Act violation for a rental property owner of four or more units to pay for the services of a 'coordinator' — a software or data analytics service that collects prices, supply, and lease-termination data from two or more landlords and recommends rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels [S2].

Makes it unlawful for such a coordinator itself to facilitate agreements among landlords not to compete, and bars coordinators from acquiring competitors when the merger would lessen competition or create a monopoly [S2].

Gives the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general enforcement authority, and lets any aggrieved person sue to recover threefold damages plus attorney fees, with the option to invalidate pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers in these cases [S2].

Eases pleading standards so tenants claiming 'consciously parallel pricing coordination' do not have to allege facts excluding independent pricing, and preserves stronger state and local laws rather than preempting them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large landlords and the rent-setting software industry. Firms selling pricing and revenue-management software to landlords would lose a core line of business, and landlords using those services would face per se antitrust liability and treble-damage lawsuits. Owners of as few as four rental units are covered, so some small and mid-size landlords face compliance risk alongside the large operators.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pricing-software firms and landlords using them

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to any owner of four or more rental units and treats buying the software service itself as a per se violation, so a small landlord who subscribes to a mainstream revenue-management tool could face treble-damage exposure even without proof of any agreement to fix rents [S2].

The per se standard and lowered pleading requirements reduce the usual defenses available in antitrust cases, which defenders of pricing software argue could chill legitimate tools that help individual landlords price competitively; the bill provides no safe harbor for such uses [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit would be direct: rents are one of the largest household expenses, and an industry-wide pricing channel that pools competitors' data is a textbook antitrust concern that existing case law handles slowly and case-by-case. The costs are real but manageable with careful enforcement — the main design risk is the four-unit coverage threshold and the per se rule sweeping in small landlords with no intent to coordinate. A narrower threshold or safe harbor could have reduced that risk. On balance, the bill's targeted purpose outweighs its compliance costs, though it was never refined through committee work.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action until the 118th Congress ended and the bill expired.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced S. 3692 with eight original co-introducers on January 30, 2024, and ten senators in total cosponsored it, all Democrats or independents [S1][S2][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the bill's only action [S1][S4].

The Judiciary Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 118th Congress, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-setting software firms and large landlords that use them are better off: the shared pricing-algorithm business model continues operating under the existing legal regime, and tenants gained no new antitrust tools. The Senate as an institution also avoided a recorded vote on the issue.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten cosponsors; took no further procedural steps available to him (such as a floor discharge attempt)

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Sen. Mazie Hirono, Sen. Laphonza Butler, and Sen. Jeff Merkley

for.name: 10 senators (9 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 4 Senate Independents)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored

against.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote on the bill during the 17 months before the Congress ended

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the bill never moved; with no Republican support, the bill had no realistic path to a floor vote even if it had cleared committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all eleven sponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill's fate was decided by inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: These firms pool pricing, supply, and lease-termination data from competing landlords and sell rent recommendations back to them — the 'coordinator' role the bill would make unlawful. Their core business model depends on exactly the cross-landlord data exchange the bill bans, and the bill's death left that model intact.

Landlords using shared pricing services would have faced per se antitrust liability and treble-damage suits from tenants; the bill's death lets them continue using these services. Even under the bill, they would have kept operating their own properties — the bill targeted the shared-pricing channel, not landlording itself.

industries.industry: Mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver agreements in residential leases
industries.note: The bill would have let tenants invalidate pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in lawsuits under the Act, removing a common shield against group claims; its death preserves those clauses in leases.
